content: The study included adults living with HIV, both male and female, aged between 22 and 66 years. Two meta-analyses were conducted across 13 subgroup comparisons. Both studies demonstrated a positive impact of combined aerobic and resistance exercise on people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA) who were on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). The overall quality of evidence, as assessed by the GRADE system, was moderate. Evidence suggested that engaging in moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (55–85% of maximum heart rate) for 30–60 minutes, 2–5 times per week, over a period of 6–24 weeks significantly improved role activity limitation and quality of life (QoL) domains compared to non-exercise groups. A meta-analysis by Gomes Neto in 2015, which included seven randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 386 participants, found a high risk of bias but no serious inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, or publication bias. This study investigated the effects of combined aerobic and resistance exercise (CARE) in HIV-infected patients from the earliest available data to August 2014. The findings consistently showed that exercise improved QoL. All studies assessing QoL reported significant improvements in the exercise group compared to controls. Mutimura (2008) reported significant improvements in psychological well-being, independence, social relationships, HIV-HAART-specific domains, and overall QoL in the exercise group, with no changes observed in the control group. Fillipas (2006) found improvements in overall health and cognitive function subscales of QoL in the exercise group. Rojas (2003) observed better improvements in five QoL subscales in the exercise group compared to controls. Maharaj (2011) reported significant improvements in physical and mental components of QoL. Mutimura (2008) also noted enhancements in psychological well-being and social interaction domains. Galantino (2005) reported improvements in the functional domain of QoL, while Ogalha (2011) found enhancements in general health, vitality, and mental health domains. However, Cade (2010) found no improvement in overall health-related QoL except for emotional well-being. These findings suggest that exercise can improve certain aspects of QoL in PLWHA, but the results are domain-specific and inconclusive. O’Brien (2016) downgraded the evidence to low quality due to performance and attrition bias, suspected publication bias, and heterogeneity in meta-analyses of subscales. However, the evidence was later upgraded to high quality due to a clear dose-response relationship. O’Brien (2010) did not downgrade the evidence despite unclear risk of bias. Nixon (2005) downgraded the evidence to low quality due to high withdrawal rates, indirectness caused by heterogeneity in outcome measures, and inconsistency in findings. O’Brien (2004) initially downgraded the evidence to low quality due to potential publication bias, attrition bias, and heterogeneity from varied exercise interventions but later upgraded it to moderate quality due to a dose-response relationship. O’Brien (2017) rated the evidence as low quality due to high risk of performance and attrition bias, inconsistency from participant variability, and heterogeneity in interventions and outcome measures. O’Brien (2008) downgraded the evidence to very low quality due to significant variation in interventions, participants, and outcomes, as well as high withdrawal rates and lack of blinding, which may have introduced the Hawthorne effect. Gomes Neto (2015) initially graded the evidence as moderate due to uncertain risk of selective reporting and lack of therapist blinding but later upgraded it to high quality due to a dose-response relationship. Bhatta (2017) graded the evidence as moderate due to serious risk of bias and indirectness, with heterogeneity in target populations, interventions, and study designs. Regarding the effects of physical activity on body composition in PLWHA, O’Brien (2016) found no significant changes in body mass index (BMI), lean body mass, or fat mass in participants engaging in aerobic or combined aerobic and resistance exercise compared to non-exercising controls. Similarly, no significant differences were observed in waist and hip circumference or waist-to-hip ratio. The evidence was graded as moderate, with no serious inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, or publication bias. Resistance exercise interventions also showed no significant changes in BMI, lean body mass, or fat mass. However, there was a potential clinically important increase in girth among resistance exercisers compared to aerobic exercisers. Heterogeneity was present in meta-analyses for arm and thigh girth. Overall, the evidence was graded as moderate, with some studies showing domain-specific improvements in QoL and body composition, but the results remain inconclusive due to heterogeneity and variability in study designs.
